title: How to Help All Teachers Become Literacy Teachers 2026
author: Corey Solitaire
summary: Corey Solitaire, a science teacher at Woodstock Union High and Middle School in Vermont, explains how his school has tried to make literacy a shared responsibility across subjects. He argues that teacher hesitation comes from training rather than disagreement, since content teachers were prepared to teach their subject, not reading, writing, speaking and academic vocabulary. The school built its approach on the 2022 IES adolescent literacy guide, Sue Szachowicz's teacher-led model from Brockton High School, Anita Archer's instructional strategies and the Goyen Foundation's Teachers Teaching Teachers protocol. Teachers volunteered to record two or three minute videos of one strategy with real students, and those clips became the basis of rotating breakout groups in schoolwide professional development. He cites encouraging state results but says he cares most about teachers asking for more reading and writing in their rooms. His conclusion is that improving literacy needs willing colleagues, not a staff of literacy experts.
points: Framing literacy as routines that support content learning, rather than a mandate to become reading teachers, removes much of the resistance from overloaded subject specialists.
The school limited itself to four areas, reading, writing, speaking and academic vocabulary, and supplied posters and simple strategies so the work was manageable on a Monday morning.
Short classroom videos of colleagues, including attempts that did not go to plan, proved a more credible professional development tool than polished training.
Teacher-led breakout groups rotating every ten minutes turned the staff's own expertise into the training, echoing the Brockton model of teacher leadership.
The author's evidence of success goes beyond state test results to teachers requesting more literacy work and students seeing reading as part of science.
quotes: The key takeaway is that the goal was never to turn every teacher into a reading teacher, but to help ALL teachers understand how developing new routines around reading, writing, and speaking help to support the learning we are already asking students to do.
Most, if not all, of us received little training in reading, writing, speaking, or using academic vocabulary within our content areas.

Yes, math teachers are still math teachers and science teachers are still science teachers, but all the work we do depends on students being able to read, write, and talk about what they are learning.

Nobody needed another initiative that sounded great in a meeting but was difficult to put into practice on a Monday morning. We focused on four areas: Reading, Writing, Speaking, and Academic Vocabulary.
These were not polished training videos with multiple takes or teachers trying to deliver the perfect lesson. They were real teachers working with real students in their own classrooms.
The expertise is already in the room. We just needed to create opportunities for teachers to share what they know and learn from one another.
The good news is that none of this requires a school full of literacy experts. It requires teachers who are willing to try something, see how it works, and make adjustments along the way.
